I've been running a trading bot on my TG for a while now and have used @digitalocean and other services to store its trading logs and market data.

As that history grows, I realized that I need to keep a copy separate from the server running the bot, so I don't lose it if I move the bot to another server or rebuild its setup.

I also want to be able to reuse that history if I change tools or try another AI model, rather than starting from scratch.

@WalrusProtocol launched Walrus Console, and what caught my attention was the decentralized storage aspect.

The data is distributed across independent storage operators, so the network is designed to keep stored files accessible even when some operators go offline.

It brings the files, API access, encryption, and access controls into one place, which sounds easier than bouncing between other services (which I've been doing, and it sucks ngl).

I saw that they're currently offering 5GB of free storage, so I created an API key, and I'm going through the process of connecting it to my bot.

I'll let you know how it goes.

Disclosure: I'm a $WAL holder.

80% of us will trust an AI answer even if it's false (⁠╥⁠﹏⁠╥⁠)

Found a great independent study on how people follow advice from LLMs, and the results are very frustrating.

Here’s what they did:

1,372 participants answered seven Cognitive Reflection Test trick questions (9,593 total trials), either alone or with an embedded ChatGPT assistant.

The researchers controlled the assistant to give either the correct answer or a confident wrong one.

They tracked AI use, whether people followed it, accuracy, and confidence. Later studies added time pressure, then incentives plus immediate feedback.

Results:

Participants used AI on over 50% of trials and usually copied it, following correct AI ~93% of the time and wrong AI ~80%.

AI also boosted confidence even when wrong.

Ouch.

thread_tweets.text:
Some choice quotes from the report: 

Banks as cops: these efforts distracted the banks from objective assessments of financial risks and increased the risk of misuse by some to refuse service to subjectively disfavored customers or industries. Moreover, it put banks in a quasi-legislative position of limiting banking services—or imposing values-based conditions on the availability of banking services—for lawful businesses disfavored by some activists and political leaders who lack the legal basis or legislative power to restrict or outlaw these business activities

Mere allegations: Mere allegations, negative press, or negative reviews contributed to some banks declining to serve average Americans, even in the absence of any validation of the underlying facts or concerns; yet some banks were able to find ways to get comfortable with the reputation risks posed by high-net-worth clients.

Inconsistency: The OCC found that, in response to general reputation risk policies, bank employees escalated customers or prospective customers that held potentially contested viewpoints outside the perceived “mainstream” and that those views were often equated with higher potential reputation risk. The OCC found that decisions related to such escalations were not universally consistent across transactions the OCC sampled, illustrating the subjective nature of the banks’ ambiguous and open-ended reputation risk policies

NGOs: The banks also relied on various sources to inform these decisions, including the results of negative news searches and non-traditional sources, such as the opinions of advocacy organizations

Whipsaw: When banks rely on difficult-to-quantify factors to decide whether to provide financial services, there is significant risk that bank decisions will whipsaw back and forth with the current political or social climate. This report confirms that value judgments and assumptions regarding the current views held by elected officials and policy makers can factor into banks’ decision making. The report also observes that as the political and social climate changed, so too did banks’ application of industry restrictions. Past experience suggests that industries may continue to suffer this whipsaw effect with the change of each administration or Congress, even in the absence of statutory changes.

I see endless people on X giving investment advice, arguing about stocks, and sharing their shitty stock picks.

Maybe your stock selection is poor. Maybe your research doesn’t work. Maybe you don’t understand position sizing or risk management.

Before you send me or anyone else a DM with a stock you think we should research, please include your trading track record over the past 5–10 years.

Show us by how much you’ve outperformed the S&P 500.

Then I might be interested.

If you haven’t beaten the index over five years, perhaps finding great stocks isn’t something you’re good at yet-it’s a fact. And that’s fine, as long as you’re willing to recognize it.

I don’t believe in fixed strategies or becoming attached to opinions. I believe in adapting, learning, and following the religion of logic.

Unlike professional sports, where your body eventually declines, trading is something you can keep getting better at throughout your life.

But only if you’re willing to admit when you’re wrong.

And until you have something to teach, maybe the best thing you can do is shut up, listen, ask questions, and 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗲.

That’s radical honesty, and I think it’s one of the most important qualities in trading.

I think many people on X misunderstand this.

If you look at history, some of the best companies in the world have experienced 80% drawdowns.

I know the $WGS story very well. At one point, it represented more than 40% of my portfolio, and I trimmed it too.

The stock went to $100 and then all the way back to $60. That’s what stocks do.

This is why I believe you need to actively manage large positions, especially after big runs.

Obviously, if you have a five-year time horizon, you might not care about these swings. But when a stock becomes a huge part of your portfolio, you have to manage that risk somehow.

My style is not to buy and hold forever through massive drawdowns.

Some investors prefer to buy and never touch their positions. I prefer to actively manage mine.

Neither approach is necessarily wrong. It’s simply a matter of personal investment style and risk management.

i wanted a physical version of my ai agent. Something real in the living room that shows my to-do list and my day, and that my wife can see too.

I bought a seeed reterminal e1002, an e-ink display. e-ink because it looks like paper: no glow, no buzz, it just sits there like a note on the wall (almost)

setup was honestly simple:
- built the open-source muse gadget firmware on my computer with my sdk token in it
- flashed it to the device over usb
- paired it in the muse app (settings, devices, developer mode) thanks @natfriedman 

now every morning at 7am my agent renders my briefing (calendar, top to-dos, weather) and pushes it to the screen. my wife reads it over coffee. it basically became the family's shared to-do list

whole thing took ~20 min. your agent doesn't have to live in a chat window. give it a physical representation!
